rows.name: Asano Naganori attacks Kira Yoshinaka in the Pine Corridor
rows.desc: The lord of Akō drew his sword on the master of ceremonies Kira inside Edo Castle and was ordered to commit seppuku the same day.

rows.name: Asano Naganori
rows.desc: The lord of Akō committed seppuku at the Tamura mansion in Shiba after the attack in the castle.

rows.name: Forty-seven rōnin raid Kira's mansion
rows.desc: Former Akō retainers led by Ōishi Yoshio stormed Kira's residence in Honjo, killed him and carried his head to Sengaku-ji.

rows.name: Kira Yoshinaka
rows.desc: The shogunate master of ceremonies was killed by the Akō rōnin in his Honjo residence.

rows.name: Seppuku of the Akō rōnin
rows.desc: The shogunate ordered the rōnin, held in four daimyo mansions, to commit seppuku; Ōishi died at the Hosokawa mansion in Takanawa.

rows.name: Ōishi Yoshio
rows.desc: The leader of the Akō vendetta committed seppuku and was buried beside his lord at Sengaku-ji.

rows.name: Rōnin buried at Sengaku-ji
rows.desc: The forty-six who committed seppuku were buried beside Asano Naganori, making the temple a place of pilgrimage.

rows.name: Genroku Kantō earthquake
rows.desc: A great earthquake and tsunami struck Sagami Bay and the Bōsō coast, wrecking Odawara castle town and killing thousands.

rows.name: Hōei eruption of Mount Fuji
rows.desc: Fuji's last eruption buried Subashiri and other villages on its eastern slope under deep ash and scoria.

rows.name: Fuji ash falls on Edo
rows.desc: Ash from the Hōei eruption darkened the sky and settled in a layer over Edo, about 100 km away.

rows.name: Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu
rows.desc: Tsunayoshi's favorite held Kawagoe domain and developed the Santome new fields on the Musashino plateau.

rows.name: Rikugien garden completed
rows.desc: Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu finished his stroll garden at Komagome after seven years of work.

rows.name: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi
rows.desc: The fifth shogun died; his laws protecting animals were repealed soon after.

rows.name: Nakano dog kennels abolished
rows.desc: The huge shelters built for stray dogs under Tsunayoshi's Laws of Compassion were closed by Ienobu.

rows.name: Tokugawa Ienobu
rows.desc: The sixth shogun ruled with the scholar Arai Hakuseki as his chief adviser.

rows.name: Arai Hakuseki
rows.desc: The Confucian scholar shaped shogunate policy on coinage, trade and protocol under Ienobu and Ietsugu.

rows.name: Arai Hakuseki questions Giovanni Sidotti
rows.desc: Hakuseki interviewed the Sicilian missionary held at the Kirishitan Yashiki, material he used for Seiyō Kibun.

rows.name: Giovanni Battista Sidotti
rows.desc: The last Catholic missionary to enter Edo-period Japan died in confinement at the Christian mansion.

rows.name: Seiyō Kibun
rows.desc: Arai Hakuseki's account of the West, drawn from his questioning of Sidotti.

rows.name: Hama Goten shogunal villa
rows.desc: The Kōfu Tokugawa seaside estate became a shogunal villa when Ienobu took office.

rows.name: Korean embassy received by Ienobu
rows.desc: A Joseon mission reached Edo, and Hakuseki revised the reception protocol and the shogun's title.

rows.name: Shōtoku recoinage
rows.desc: On Hakuseki's advice the shogunate restored the gold content of coins debased under Tsunayoshi.

rows.name: Ejima-Ikushima affair
rows.desc: An Ōoku lady-in-waiting's visit to the kabuki actor Ikushima Shingorō led to some 1,300 punishments and the closure of the Yamamura-za.

rows.name: Sukeroku first staged
rows.desc: Ichikawa Danjūrō II first played the dandy Sukeroku, later one of the Kabuki Jūhachiban.

rows.name: Ichikawa Danjūrō I
rows.desc: The founder of the aragoto acting style was stabbed to death on stage by a fellow actor.

rows.name: Kōmyōdō main hall at Narita
rows.desc: A new main hall was built at Naritasan Shinshō-ji, a temple tied to the Ichikawa Danjūrō acting line.

rows.name: Narita three-storied pagoda
rows.desc: The painted three-storied pagoda of Shinshō-ji was completed.

rows.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune
rows.desc: The eighth shogun launched the Kyōhō reforms to restore shogunal finances.

rows.name: Kyōhō reforms begin
rows.desc: Yoshimune began a program of frugality, new fields, rice price management and legal codification.

rows.name: Ōoka Tadasuke
rows.desc: As South machi-bugyō, Ōoka became famed for judgments and organized Edo's town firefighters.

rows.name: Iroha town fire brigades
rows.desc: Ōoka organized Edo townsmen into named machi-bikeshi brigades, identified by the iroha syllabary.

rows.name: Ban on Western books relaxed
rows.desc: Yoshimune allowed imports of Chinese translations of Western books not about Christianity, opening the way for Dutch learning.

rows.name: Uraga magistracy established
rows.desc: The shogunate moved its ship inspection post from Shimoda to Uraga at the mouth of Edo Bay.

rows.name: Cherry trees planted on Asukayama
rows.desc: Yoshimune had cherries planted on the hill and opened it to commoners as a blossom-viewing ground.

rows.name: Meyasubako petition box
rows.desc: Yoshimune placed a box outside the Hyōjōsho where commoners could submit signed petitions.

rows.name: Minkan Seiyō
rows.desc: Tanaka Kyūgu, headman of Kawasaki post town, wrote this advice book on rural administration, which reached Yoshimune.

rows.name: Koishikawa Yōjōsho
rows.desc: Following a petition through the box, a free clinic for the poor opened in the shogunal herb garden.

rows.name: Ogyū Sorai
rows.desc: The Confucian philosopher taught his Ken'en school at Kayabachō and advised Yoshimune.

rows.name: Seidan
rows.desc: Ogyū Sorai's political memorial to Yoshimune on government and the samurai economy.

rows.name: Arai Hakuseki
rows.desc: Hakuseki died in retirement in Edo.

rows.name: Ogyū Sorai
rows.desc: The founder of the Kobunjigaku school died in Edo.

rows.name: Minuma Tsūsen-bori
rows.desc: Izawa Yasobei completed Japan's oldest lock canal, linking the Minuma irrigation channels with the Shiba river.

rows.name: Kyōhō uchikowashi
rows.desc: After the Kyōhō famine pushed up rice prices, Edo townspeople smashed the house of rice merchant Takama Denbei, the city's first great house-smashing.

rows.name: First Ryōgoku river-opening fireworks
rows.desc: Fireworks at Ryōgoku began as a memorial for victims of famine and epidemic, the origin of the Sumida fireworks.

rows.name: Aoki Kon'yō
rows.desc: Known as the sweet potato master, he trialed the crop as famine food in the Koishikawa garden for Yoshimune.

rows.name: Kujikata Osadamegaki
rows.desc: Yoshimune's code of criminal and civil procedure was compiled for the shogunate's judges.

rows.name: Daimaru opens in Edo
rows.desc: The Kyoto dry goods house Daimaru opened a branch at Ōdenmachō.

rows.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune
rows.desc: The reforming shogun died in Edo Castle six years after retiring.

rows.name: Ōoka Tadasuke
rows.desc: The famous magistrate died in Edo, months after Yoshimune.

rows.name: Korean embassy of 1748
rows.desc: A Joseon mission congratulated the new shogun Ieshige in Edo.

rows.name: Kanadehon Chūshingura in Edo
rows.desc: The puppet play retelling the Akō vendetta, premiered in Osaka the year before, reached the Edo stage.

rows.name: Kamo no Mabuchi
rows.desc: The kokugaku scholar taught in Edo and served the Tayasu house.

rows.name: Kamo no Mabuchi
rows.desc: The scholar of the Man'yōshū died in Edo.

rows.name: Ōta Nanpo
rows.desc: The comic poet and official, also known as Shokusanjin, was born in Ushigome.

rows.name: Sugita Genpaku
rows.desc: The future translator of Kaitai Shinsho was born at the Obama domain mansion in Edo.

rows.name: Tokugawa Ieharu
rows.desc: The future tenth shogun was born in Edo Castle.

rows.name: Matsudaira Sadanobu
rows.desc: Yoshimune's grandson was born in the Tayasu Tokugawa house in Edo.

rows.name: Katsushika Hokusai
rows.desc: Hokusai was born in the Warigesui district of Honjo, Katsushika.

rows.name: Santō Kyōden
rows.desc: The writer and print designer was born in Fukagawa.

rows.name: Sakai Hōitsu
rows.desc: The Rinpa painter was born into the Himeji Sakai family at their Edo mansion.

rows.name: Tani Bunchō
rows.desc: The literati painter was born in Edo to a Tayasu retainer.

rows.name: Kyokutei Bakin
rows.desc: The author of Hakkenden was born in Fukagawa.

rows.name: Harunobu's first full-color nishiki-e
rows.desc: Calendar prints designed by Suzuki Harunobu launched multi-block full-color woodblock printing in Edo.

rows.name: Suzuki Harunobu
rows.desc: The pioneer of nishiki-e died in Edo.

rows.name: Kozukappara dissection
rows.desc: Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku and Nakagawa Jun'an watched a dissection and found the Dutch anatomy book exact.

rows.name: Great Meiwa fire
rows.desc: A fire set at Daien-ji in Meguro swept across Edo to Asakusa, one of the city's three great fires.

rows.name: Tanuma Okitsugu
rows.desc: As rōjū Tanuma promoted guilds, trade, mining and the drainage of Inba marsh.

rows.name: Naitō-Shinjuku reopened
rows.desc: The Kōshū Kaidō post station at Shinjuku, closed in 1718, was revived.

rows.name: Kaitai Shinsho
rows.desc: Sugita Genpaku and colleagues published their translation of a Dutch anatomy text, founding rangaku medicine.

rows.name: Carl Peter Thunberg
rows.desc: The Swedish botanist accompanied the Dutch mission to Edo and met Japanese physicians there.

rows.name: Hiraga Gennai's erekiteru
rows.desc: Gennai restored a Dutch electrostatic generator and showed it in Edo.

rows.name: Hiraga Gennai
rows.desc: The polymath died in the Denmachō jail after killing a man.

rows.name: Kobayashi Issa
rows.desc: The haiku poet lived and worked in Edo from age fourteen until returning to Shinano.

rows.name: Shiba Kōkan's first copperplate etching
rows.desc: The painter made Japan's first copperplate etching, a view of Mimeguri shrine.

rows.name: Tsutaya Jūzaburō opens in Nihonbashi
rows.desc: The publisher of Utamaro and Sharaku moved his shop from Yoshiwara to Tōriabura-chō.

rows.name: Inba marsh drainage
rows.desc: Tanuma began draining Inba marsh for new rice land; a great flood in 1786 wrecked the works.

rows.name: Tanuma Okitomo stabbed in Edo Castle
rows.desc: The junior councillor, son of Tanuma Okitsugu, was cut down by the bannerman Sano Masakoto.

rows.name: Tenmei famine
rows.desc: Cold years and the 1783 Asama eruption brought famine; refugees and high prices hit Edo.

rows.name: Shirandō Dutch school
rows.desc: Ōtsuki Gentaku opened a private school of Dutch studies in Edo.

rows.name: Tenmei flood
rows.desc: Heavy rain flooded the Kantō plain and the low wards of Edo.

rows.name: Tenmei uchikowashi in Edo
rows.desc: Crowds sacked rice dealers across Edo for days, helping topple Tanuma's faction.

rows.name: Ninomiya Sontoku
rows.desc: The peasant reformer was born in Kayama village near Odawara.

rows.name: Matsudaira Sadanobu
rows.desc: Sadanobu led the shogunate and carried out the Kansei reforms.

rows.name: Kansei reforms
rows.desc: Sadanobu imposed austerity, relief granaries, debt cancellation for bannermen and moral controls.

rows.name: Tokugawa Ienari
rows.desc: The eleventh shogun reigned for fifty years, the longest of the Tokugawa.

rows.name: Tanuma Okitsugu
rows.desc: The fallen rōjū died in Edo stripped of most of his lands.

rows.name: First yokozuna licenses
rows.desc: Tanikaze and Onogawa received yokozuna licenses, marking the rise of sumo as Edo's great sport.

rows.name: Kansei Prohibition of heterodox learning
rows.desc: The Hayashi school was told to teach only Zhu Xi Confucianism.

rows.name: Ishikawajima laborers' camp
rows.desc: Hasegawa Heizō set up a workhouse to train the homeless and petty offenders.

rows.name: Hasegawa Heizō
rows.desc: The arson and theft commissioner policed Edo and ran the Ishikawajima workhouse.

rows.name: Santō Kyōden punished
rows.desc: Kyōden was put in manacles for fifty days and Tsutaya fined over sharebon set in the pleasure quarter.

rows.name: Utamaro's bust portraits of beauties
rows.desc: Utamaro's okubi-e portraits of women, published by Tsutaya, defined the age of beauty prints.

rows.name: Wagaku Kōdansho
rows.desc: The blind scholar Hanawa Hokiichi founded an institute for Japanese studies under shogunal patronage.

rows.name: Sharaku's actor prints
rows.desc: In about ten months Tōshūsai Sharaku produced some 140 kabuki actor prints, then vanished.

rows.name: Tanikaze Kajinosuke
rows.desc: The yokozuna died in Edo of influenza while still active.

rows.name: Inō Tadataka
rows.desc: After retiring from business in Sawara, Inō studied astronomy in Edo and set out from Fukagawa to survey Japan.

rows.name: Shōheizaka Gakumonjo
rows.desc: The Hayashi academy at Yushima became the official shogunal school.

rows.name: Tsutaya Jūzaburō
rows.desc: The great publisher of ukiyo-e and popular fiction died in Edo.

rows.name: Utagawa Hiroshige
rows.desc: Hiroshige was born to a fire-warden family at Yayosu quay.

rows.name: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
rows.desc: The print designer was born to a silk dyer in Nihonbashi.

rows.name: Silver mint moved to Kakigarachō
rows.desc: The Edo Ginza silver mint was transferred from its original site to Kakigarachō.

rows.name: Tōkaidōchū Hizakurige
rows.desc: Jippensha Ikku began his comic tale of Yaji and Kita walking the Tōkaidō from Edo.

rows.name: Mukōjima Hyakkaen
rows.desc: The antique dealer Sawara Kikuu opened a flower garden that became a resort for writers.

rows.name: Great Bunka fire
rows.desc: A fire from Shiba burned through Kyōbashi, Nihonbashi and Kanda.

rows.name: Kitagawa Utamaro
rows.desc: Utamaro died in Edo, two years after being manacled over prints of Hideyoshi.

rows.name: Ukiyoburo
rows.desc: Shikitei Sanba's comic novel recorded the talk of commoners at an Edo public bath.

rows.name: Nansō Satomi Hakkenden
rows.desc: Bakin began his 106-volume epic of eight dog warriors, finished in 1842.

rows.name: Rangaku Kotohajime
rows.desc: Sugita Genpaku's memoir of how he and his friends translated Kaitai Shinsho.

rows.name: Santō Kyōden
rows.desc: The writer and tobacco-pouch merchant died in Edo.

rows.name: Sugita Genpaku
rows.desc: The translator of Kaitai Shinsho died in Edo.

rows.name: Inō Tadataka
rows.desc: Inō died at Hatchōbori before his national map was finished.

rows.name: Dai Nihon Enkai Yochi Zenzu
rows.desc: Inō's pupils completed and presented his great survey map of Japan's coasts.

rows.name: Hanawa Hokiichi
rows.desc: The compiler of Gunsho Ruijū died in Edo.

rows.name: Ōta Nanpo
rows.desc: The comic poet and official died in Edo.

rows.name: Katsu Kaishū
rows.desc: The future naval leader was born in Honjo Kamezawa.

rows.name: Tōkaidō Yotsuya Kaidan premieres
rows.desc: Tsuruya Nanboku IV's ghost play opened at the Nakamura-za.

rows.name: Philipp Franz von Siebold
rows.desc: Siebold stayed at the Nagasakiya with the Dutch court journey and met Edo scholars.

rows.name: Akamon of the Kaga mansion
rows.desc: The red gate was built for Ienari's daughter's marriage into the Maeda house.

rows.name: Tsurugaoka Hachimangū main shrine rebuilt
rows.desc: Ienari rebuilt the main hall of Kamakura's great shrine.

rows.name: Siebold incident
rows.desc: Court astronomer Takahashi Kageyasu was arrested for giving Siebold maps; he died in prison in 1829.

rows.name: Sakai Hōitsu
rows.desc: The Rinpa painter died at his Uka-an studio in Negishi.

rows.name: Bunsei great fire
rows.desc: A fire from Kanda Sakumachō burned much of downtown Edo.

rows.name: Tsuruya Nanboku IV
rows.desc: The author of Yotsuya Kaidan died in Edo.

rows.name: Nise Murasaki Inaka Genji
rows.desc: Ryūtei Tanehiko's illustrated retelling of Genji became a bestseller until banned in 1842.

rows.name: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
rows.desc: Hokusai's landscape series, published by Nishimuraya, used imported Prussian blue.

rows.name: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
rows.desc: Hokusai's print showed boats under a breaking wave off Kanagawa with Fuji beyond.

rows.name: Jippensha Ikku
rows.desc: The author of Hizakurige died in Edo.

rows.name: Kawanabe Kyōsai
rows.desc: The painter and caricaturist was born in Koga, Shimōsa.

rows.name: Kabuki Jūhachiban announced
rows.desc: Ichikawa Danjūrō VII named his family's eighteen great plays.

rows.name: Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō
rows.desc: Hiroshige's series beginning at Nihonbashi made him the master of landscape prints.
rows.wikipedia: The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō

rows.name: Ekōin becomes sumo's home
rows.desc: Charity sumo tournaments were regularly held at Ekōin temple in Ryōgoku.

rows.name: Tenpō famine
rows.desc: Years of cold and failed harvests caused hunger, epidemics and relief huts in Edo.

rows.name: Edo Meisho Zue
rows.desc: The Saitō family's illustrated gazetteer of famous places, with art by Hasegawa Settan.

rows.name: Kondō Isami
rows.desc: The future Shinsengumi commander was born in Kami-Ishihara, Tama.

rows.name: Hijikata Toshizō
rows.desc: The future Shinsengumi vice commander was born in Ishida village, Hino.

rows.name: Egawa Hidetatsu
rows.desc: The Nirayama intendant studied Western gunnery and coastal defense.

rows.name: Enomoto Takeaki
rows.desc: The future shogunal naval commander was born in Shitaya.

rows.name: Tokugawa Yoshinobu
rows.desc: The last shogun was born at the Mito domain residence in Koishikawa.

rows.name: Morrison incident
rows.desc: Shore batteries at Uraga fired on the American ship Morrison, which was returning castaways.

rows.name: Portrait of Takami Senseki
rows.desc: Watanabe Kazan painted the Koga domain elder in a Western-influenced style.

rows.name: Bansha no goku
rows.desc: Watanabe Kazan and Takano Chōei were arrested for criticizing the shogunate's expulsion policy.

rows.name: Tōyama Kagemoto
rows.desc: The future folk hero Tōyama no Kin-san became North town magistrate.

rows.name: Tani Bunchō
rows.desc: The literati painter died in Edo.

rows.name: Mizuno Tadakuni
rows.desc: Mizuno pressed the Tenpō reforms of thrift, price control and censorship.

rows.name: Tenpō reforms
rows.desc: Mizuno dissolved merchant guilds, banned luxury and restricted theatre and fiction.

rows.name: Theatres moved to Saruwaka-chō
rows.desc: The kabuki theatres were forced out of the city centre to Saruwaka-chō near Asakusa.

rows.name: Ichikawa Danjūrō VII banished
rows.desc: The great actor was exiled from Edo for luxury under the Tenpō reforms.

rows.name: Ryūtei Tanehiko
rows.desc: Tanehiko died soon after his Inaka Genji was banned.

rows.name: Juntendō medical school
rows.desc: Satō Taizen opened a Western medicine school and clinic in Sakura domain.

rows.name: Crowd stones Mizuno's mansion
rows.desc: After the failed Agechi-rei land order Mizuno was dismissed and Edo crowds attacked his residence.

rows.name: Abe Masahiro
rows.desc: As head of the rōjū Abe handled the Perry crisis and consulted the daimyo.

rows.name: Biddle at Uraga
rows.desc: Commodore James Biddle anchored off Uraga with two warships and was refused a treaty.

rows.name: Tokugawa Iemochi
rows.desc: The future fourteenth shogun was born at the Kii domain residence in Edo.

rows.name: Kyokutei Bakin
rows.desc: Bakin died in Edo, having finished Hakkenden while going blind.

rows.name: Katsushika Hokusai
rows.desc: Hokusai died in Asakusa aged 88.

rows.name: Takano Chōei
rows.desc: The rangaku physician, an escaped prisoner, died when officers found him in Aoyama.

rows.name: Sakuma Shōzan
rows.desc: Shōzan taught Western gunnery at Kobikichō to students including Yoshida Shōin and Katsu Kaishū.

rows.name: Hanayashiki
rows.desc: A flower garden opened behind Sensō-ji that became Japan's oldest amusement park.

rows.name: Perry's black ships at Uraga
rows.desc: Commodore Perry's squadron anchored off Uraga demanding the delivery of a letter from President Fillmore.

rows.name: Perry lands at Kurihama
rows.desc: Perry went ashore and handed Fillmore's letter to shogunate officials.

rows.name: Shinagawa Daiba batteries
rows.desc: Egawa Hidetatsu designed island batteries in Edo Bay to defend the city.

rows.name: Ishikawajima shipyard
rows.desc: The Mito domain opened a Western-style shipyard on Ishikawajima.

rows.name: Tokugawa Iesada
rows.desc: The thirteenth shogun reigned through the opening of Japan.

rows.name: Convention of Kanagawa
rows.desc: Perry and shogunate officials signed the first treaty with the United States at Yokohama village.

rows.name: Yokohama Foreign General Cemetery
rows.desc: The burial of a US Marine from Perry's fleet began the foreign cemetery.

rows.name: Nirayama reverberatory furnace
rows.desc: Work began on a furnace for casting iron cannon, completed in 1857 after Egawa's death.

rows.name: Ansei Edo earthquake
rows.desc: A strong quake and fires killed thousands in Edo, worst in the low wards east of the castle.

rows.name: Fujita Tōko
rows.desc: The Mito scholar was killed by a falling beam in the Mito residence during the earthquake.

rows.name: Namazu-e catfish prints
rows.desc: Hundreds of unlicensed prints blamed or mocked the giant catfish thought to cause earthquakes.

rows.name: Egawa Hidetatsu
rows.desc: The gunnery reformer died in Edo.

rows.name: Bansho Shirabesho
rows.desc: The shogunate founded an institute for translating and teaching Western books at Kudanshita.

rows.name: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
rows.desc: Hiroshige's last series included Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi.
rows.wikipedia: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo

rows.name: Townsend Harris
rows.desc: The American minister moved his legation from Shimoda to Zenpuku-ji in Azabu.

rows.name: Harris Treaty signed
rows.desc: Shogunate envoys signed the Treaty of Amity and Commerce aboard USS Powhatan in Edo Bay.
rows.wikipedia: Treaty of Amity and Commerce (United States–Japan)

rows.name: Ii Naosuke
rows.desc: As tairō Ii signed the commercial treaties and purged opponents.

rows.name: Cholera in Edo
rows.desc: Cholera reached Edo in late summer and killed many thousands.

rows.name: Utagawa Hiroshige
rows.desc: Hiroshige died in Edo, probably of cholera.

rows.name: Tokugawa Iesada
rows.desc: The thirteenth shogun died in Edo Castle.

rows.name: Fukuzawa's Dutch school
rows.desc: Fukuzawa Yukichi began teaching at the Nakatsu domain residence in Teppōzu, origin of Keiō.

rows.name: Otamagaike vaccination center
rows.desc: Edo rangaku physicians opened a smallpox vaccination house, forerunner of the University of Tokyo medical school.

rows.name: Yokohama opened to trade
rows.desc: The shogunate opened a new port at Yokohama instead of the treaty town of Kanagawa.

rows.name: James Curtis Hepburn
rows.desc: The American physician and missionary settled at Jōbutsu-ji in Kanagawa.

rows.name: Rutherford Alcock
rows.desc: The first British minister set up the legation at Tōzen-ji.

rows.name: Yoshida Shōin
rows.desc: The Chōshū teacher was executed in the Denmachō jail during the Ansei purge.

rows.name: Ansei Purge
rows.desc: Ii Naosuke punished over a hundred opponents of the treaties and his shogunal succession choice.

rows.name: Kanrin Maru sails for America
rows.desc: The shogunate warship under Katsu Kaishū left Uraga to accompany the embassy to the United States.

rows.name: Sakuradamon incident
rows.desc: Mito and Satsuma rōnin killed Ii Naosuke in the snow outside Sakurada Gate.

rows.name: Ii Naosuke
rows.desc: The tairō was killed outside Sakurada Gate.

rows.name: Henry Heusken killed
rows.desc: Harris's Dutch interpreter was cut down by anti-foreign samurai in Azabu.

rows.name: First Tōzen-ji incident
rows.desc: Mito rōnin attacked the British legation at night.

rows.name: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
rows.desc: The designer of warrior prints died in Edo.

rows.name: Japan Herald
rows.desc: Albert Hansard founded Yokohama's first English-language newspaper.

rows.name: Sakashitamon incident
rows.desc: Rōnin wounded senior councillor Andō Nobumasa outside Sakashita Gate.

rows.name: Princess Kazu marries Iemochi
rows.desc: The emperor's sister married the shogun to unite court and shogunate.

rows.name: Namamugi incident
rows.desc: Satsuma retainers killed the British merchant Charles Richardson on the Tōkaidō.

rows.name: Ernest Satow
rows.desc: The British student interpreter arrived in Yokohama and stayed through the Restoration.

rows.name: British legation at Gotenyama burned
rows.desc: Chōshū men including Takasugi Shinsaku and Itō Hirobumi set fire to the unfinished legation.

rows.name: Rōshigumi gather at Denzū-in
rows.desc: Masterless samurai recruited to guard the shogun gathered before leaving for Kyoto; some became the Shinsengumi.

rows.name: Kiyokawa Hachirō
rows.desc: The founder of the Rōshigumi was assassinated in Azabu.

rows.name: Felice Beato
rows.desc: The photographer settled in Yokohama and recorded Japan for two decades.

rows.name: Yokosuka iron works
rows.desc: Construction began on a French-designed arsenal under Léonce Verny.

rows.name: Utagawa Kunisada
rows.desc: The most prolific ukiyo-e designer died in Edo.

rows.name: Great Yokohama fire
rows.desc: A fire destroyed much of the Japanese town and part of the foreign settlement.

rows.name: Hepburn's Japanese-English dictionary
rows.desc: Hepburn's Waei Gorin Shūsei, compiled in Yokohama, popularized his romanization.

rows.name: Tokugawa Yoshinobu
rows.desc: The last shogun surrendered power to the court in late 1867.

rows.name: Satsuma Edo mansion burned
rows.desc: Shogunate forces burned the Satsuma residence after its agents provoked unrest, helping start the Boshin war.

rows.name: Saigō and Katsu meet
rows.desc: Saigō Takamori and Katsu Kaishū agreed on the peaceful surrender of Edo.

rows.name: Edo Castle surrendered
rows.desc: Imperial forces took over Edo Castle without fighting.

rows.name: Kondō Isami captured at Nagareyama
rows.desc: The Shinsengumi commander surrendered to imperial troops at Nagareyama.

rows.name: Kondō Isami
rows.desc: Kondō was beheaded at Itabashi.

rows.name: Battle of Ueno
rows.desc: Imperial troops crushed the Shōgitai at Kan'ei-ji with Armstrong guns.

rows.name: Kan'ei-ji burned
rows.desc: Most of the Tokugawa temple at Ueno was destroyed in the fighting.

rows.name: Edo renamed Tokyo
rows.desc: An imperial edict renamed Edo the Eastern Capital.

rows.name: Emperor Meiji enters Tokyo
rows.desc: The young emperor arrived and took Edo Castle as his residence.

rows.name: Tsukiji Hotel
rows.desc: Shimizu Kisuke built a Western-style hotel for the new Tsukiji foreign settlement.

rows.name: Ōyama pilgrimage
rows.desc: Edo commoners formed confraternities for summer pilgrimage to Ōyama Afuri Shrine.

rows.name: Nokogiriyama 1500 rakan
rows.desc: Ōno Jinroku and his pupils carved the stone arhats at Nihon-ji over two decades.

rows.name: Ninomiya Sontoku
rows.desc: Sontoku restored the finances of the Hattori family, Odawara domain elders.

rows.name: Asama ash on the Kantō
rows.desc: The Tenmei eruption of Asama spread ash over northern Kantō and worsened the famine.

rows.name: Senju vegetable market
rows.desc: Senju post town on the Nikkō road hosted one of Edo's three great produce markets.

rows.name: Morisada Mankō
rows.desc: Kitagawa Morisada began his encyclopedia of customs comparing Edo with Kyoto and Osaka.
